“Chiefly Mr. Bulstrode’s unpopularity, to begin with. Half the town would
almost take trouble for the sake of thwarting him. In this stupid world most
people never consider that a thing is good to be done unless it is done by
their own set. I had no connection with Bulstrode before I came here. I look at
him quite impartially, and I see that he has some notions—that he has set
things on foot—which I can turn to good public purpose. If a fair number of the
better educated men went to work with the belief that their observations might
contribute to the reform of medical doctrine and practice, we should soon see a
change for the better. That’s my point of view. I hold that by refusing to work
with Mr. Bulstrode I should be turning my back on an opportunity of making my
profession more generally serviceable.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's extended response articulates the novel's critique of provincial pettiness, the power of faction over merit, and his own idealistic philosophy about advancing medical science through institutional reform.
enrichment.best_quote: In this stupid world most people never consider that a thing is good to be done unless it is done by their own set.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate explains that Bulstrode's unpopularity fuels opposition to the hospital, and argues that refusing to work with Bulstrode would be abandoning an opportunity to improve medical practice for public benefit.

context: Lydgate explains to Dorothea why he is willing to work with the unpopular Mr. Bulstrode on the New Hospital project, despite local opposition. He argues that Bulstrode's unpopularity stems from petty town politics and religious prejudice, and that he should not refuse the opportunity to advance medical practice and serve the public good, regardless of his patron's unpopularity.

text:
“I quite agree with you,” said Dorothea, at once fascinated by the situation
sketched in Lydgate’s words. “But what is there against Mr. Bulstrode? I know
that my uncle is friendly with him.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dorothea's agreement and curiosity about Bulstrode advances the dialogue but offers limited new insight beyond her receptiveness to idealistic appeals.
enrichment.summary: Dorothea agrees with Lydgate and asks what objections exist against Bulstrode, noting her uncle's friendship with him.

context: Dorothea enthusiastically supports Lydgate's plan to establish a new hospital under Mr. Bulstrode's patronage, despite local opposition rooted in Bulstrode's unpopularity and religious reputation. enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief, deflecting response that avoids detail, serving primarily as transition rather than substantive revelation.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate briefly attributes opposition to Bulstrode's religious tone and breaks off discussion.

context: Lydgate explains to Dorothea the reasons for opposition to Mr. Bulstrode's Hospital project in Middlemarch. text:
“That is all the stronger reason for despising such an opposition,” said
Dorothea, looking at the affairs of Middlemarch by the light of the great
persecutions.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dorothea's indignant response reveals her character—idealistic and dismissive of provincial prejudice—but the line is relatively short and her perspective somewhat naive.
enrichment.best_quote: That is all the stronger reason for despising such an opposition.

context: Dorothea responds to Lydgate's explanation that people oppose Mr. Bulstrode's hospital project partly because of his religious tone. She views this opposition as petty prejudice against a man's faith, comparing it to historical religious persecutions.

text:
“To put the matter quite fairly, they have other objections to him:—he is
masterful and rather unsociable, and he is concerned with trade, which has
complaints of its own that I know nothing about. But what has that to do with
the question whether it would not be a fine thing to establish here a more
valuable hospital than any they have in the county? The immediate motive to the
opposition, however, is the fact that Bulstrode has put the medical direction
into my hands. Of course I am glad of that. It gives me an opportunity of doing
some good work,—and I am aware that I have to justify his choice of me. But the
consequence is, that the whole profession in Middlemarch have set themselves
tooth and nail against the Hospital, and not only refuse to cooperate
themselves, but try to blacken the whole affair and hinder subscriptions.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's fuller explanation of the medical profession's opposition and his own position reveals the intersection of personal ambition, professional rivalry, and public good—a key theme of the novel.
enrichment.best_quote: the whole profession in Middlemarch have set themselves tooth and nail against the Hospital, and not only refuse to cooperate themselves, but try to blacken the whole affair and hinder subscriptions.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate elaborates that while Bulstrode is masterful and unsociable, the immediate cause of opposition is his own appointment as medical director, which has united the local medical profession against the hospital.

context: Lydgate explains to Dorothea the reasons for opposition to the New Hospital in Middlemarch. While townspeople object to Mr. Bulstrode's personality and involvement in trade, the primary cause of the medical profession's hostility is Bulstrode's appointment of Lydgate as medical director. This has united the local doctors against the Hospital, causing them to refuse cooperation and actively work to damage its reputation and prevent donations.

text: “How very petty!” exclaimed Dorothea, indignantly.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief exclamation that provides minimal substance or development.
enrichment.summary: Dorothea expresses indignation at the pettiness of the opposition.

context: Dorothea reacts with indignation to Lydgate's explanation of the opposition to the New Hospital in Middlemarch, particularly the medical profession's petty resistance to his appointment as medical director, driven largely by professional jealousy and dislike of his patron Bulstrode rather than legitimate concerns about the hospital's merit.

text:
“I suppose one must expect to fight one’s way: there is hardly anything to be
done without it. And the ignorance of people about here is stupendous. I don’t
lay claim to anything else than having used some opportunities which have not
come within everybody’s reach; but there is no stifling the offence of being
young, and a new-comer, and happening to know something more than the old
inhabitants. Still, if I believe that I can set going a better method of
treatment—if I believe that I can pursue certain observations and inquiries
which may be a lasting benefit to medical practice, I should be a base truckler
if I allowed any consideration of personal comfort to hinder me. And the course
is all the clearer from there being no salary in question to put my persistence
in an equivocal light.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's passionate articulation of his struggle against provincial ignorance and his commitment to medical reform reveals his character, idealism, and the novel's engagement with vocation and the conflict between personal comfort and public good.
enrichment.best_quote: I should be a base truckler if I allowed any consideration of personal comfort to hinder me.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate argues that professional opposition is inevitable and reflects provincial ignorance, but asserts he will not compromise his commitment to medical reform for personal comfort.

context: Lydgate defends his commitment to establishing the New Hospital and justifies working with Bulstrode despite local opposition, explaining that he must overcome prejudice against his youth and newcomer status to pursue his medical innovations and reform of medical practice.

text:
“I am glad you have told me this, Mr. Lydgate,” said Dorothea, cordially. “I
feel sure I can help a little. I have some money, and don’t know what to do
with it—that is often an uncomfortable thought to me. I am sure I can spare two
hundred a-year for a grand purpose like this. How happy you must be, to know
things that you feel sure will do great good! I wish I could awake with that
knowledge every morning. There seems to be so much trouble taken that one can
hardly see the good of!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dorothea's offer of financial support and her poignant expression of her own unfulfilled aspirations create an important moment revealing her character, her marriage's constraints, and her capacity for idealistic action.
enrichment.best_quote: I have some money, and don't know what to do with it—that is often an uncomfortable thought to me.
enrichment.summary: Dorothea enthusiastically pledges two hundred pounds annually to the hospital and expresses her longing to possess Lydgate's sense of purposeful knowledge.

context: Dorothea offers financial support to Lydgate's hospital initiative after he explains the opposition it faces from Middlemarch's medical establishment and townspeople who resent Mr. Bulstrode's influence. She expresses both her desire to do good and her uncertainty about finding meaningful purpose in her married life.

text:
There was a melancholy cadence in Dorothea’s voice as she spoke these last
words. But she presently added, more cheerfully, “Pray come to Lowick and tell
us more of this. I will mention the subject to Mr. Casaubon. I must hasten home
now.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: The narrator's observation of melancholy in Dorothea's voice, followed by her redirection to discussing Casaubon, reveals emotional complexity but transitions back to routine action.
enrichment.summary: Dorothea's melancholy tone suggests inner conflict, but she recovers cheerfully and invites Lydgate to Lowick to discuss the hospital further with Casaubon.

context: Dorothea has just offered to donate two hundred pounds annually to Lydgate's Hospital project after he explained the opposition it faces from Middlemarch's medical establishment and townspeople, who resent Mr. Bulstrode's involvement and Lydgate's youth and influence. She now prepares to leave and promises to discuss the matter with her husband, Mr. Casaubon.

text:
She did mention it that evening, and said that she should like to subscribe two
hundred a-year—she had seven hundred a-year as the equivalent of her own
fortune, settled on her at her marriage. Mr. Casaubon made no objection beyond
a passing remark that the sum might be disproportionate in relation to other
good objects, but when Dorothea in her ignorance resisted that suggestion, he
acquiesced. He did not care himself about spending money, and was not reluctant
to give it. If he ever felt keenly any question of money it was through the
medium of another passion than the love of material property.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The narration of Dorothea's financial autonomy and Casaubon's detached acquiescence reveals marital dynamics and Casaubon's psychological state, with the final sentence providing philosophical depth about his inner life.
enrichment.best_quote: If he ever felt keenly any question of money it was through the medium of another passion than the love of material property.
enrichment.summary: Dorothea announces her pledge to subscribe two hundred pounds annually from her own settled income; Casaubon acquiesces without objection, revealing his emotional detachment from financial concerns.

context: Dorothea has just promised Lydgate two hundred pounds a year for the New Hospital after learning about the medical establishment's opposition to it. That evening, she informs her husband Mr. Casaubon of her intention to subscribe this amount from her own seven-hundred-pound annual fortune. Though he offers a mild objection about proportionality to other charitable causes, he acquiesces when Dorothea resists, revealing his indifference to money matters and the emotional distance growing between them.

text:
Dorothea told him that she had seen Lydgate, and recited the gist of her
conversation with him about the Hospital. Mr. Casaubon did not question her
further, but he felt sure that she had wished to know what had passed between
Lydgate and himself. “She knows that I know,” said the ever-restless voice
within; but that increase of tacit knowledge only thrust further off any
confidence between them. He distrusted her affection; and what loneliness is
more lonely than distrust?

enrichment.interest_rationale: This passage crystallizes the novel's central concern with marriage, knowledge, and isolation. Casaubon's suspicious interpretation of Dorothea's openness and the narrator's final philosophical question about the loneliness of distrust represent the novel's deepest thematic engagement and most profound emotional register.
enrichment.best_quote: what loneliness is more lonely than distrust?
enrichment.summary: Dorothea recounts her conversation with Lydgate to Casaubon, but his interpretation of her openness reveals his distrust of her affection, and the narrator reflects philosophically on the isolation created by suspicion.

context: Dorothea has just returned home to Lowick after her walk with Lydgate, during which she learned about the New Hospital project and Lydgate's struggles with local medical opposition. She shares the details of their conversation with her husband Mr. Casaubon and offers to contribute two hundred pounds annually to the hospital. However, Casaubon misinterprets her account, suspecting she wants to know what passed between him and Lydgate, and his distrust deepens the emotional distance between them.

text:
It is the humor of many heads to extol the days of their forefathers, and
declaim against the wickedness of times present. Which notwithstanding they
cannot handsomely do, without the borrowed help and satire of times past;
condemning the vices of their own times, by the expressions of vices in times
which they commend, which cannot but argue the community of vice in both.
Horace, therefore, Juvenal, and Persius, were no prophets, although their lines
did seem to indigitate and point at our times.—SIR THOMAS BROWNE:
 Pseudodoxia Epidemica .

enrichment.interest_rationale: An epigraph from Sir Thomas Browne on the perennial human tendency to condemn the present and idealize the past; contextual framing rather than narrative content.
enrichment.summary: Sir Thomas Browne's epigraph argues that critics who condemn modern vices often rely on historical examples that reveal the continuity of human vice across ages.

context: This epigraph appears at the beginning of the chapter and establishes the thematic framework for the ensuing narrative about Lydgate's arrival in Middlemarch. The quotation from Sir Thomas Browne argues that human vice is constant across eras, setting up Eliot's exploration of how the townspeople's opposition to Lydgate and his medical innovations mirrors timeless patterns of jealousy, prejudice, and resistance to change. It prefigures the various misconceptions and hostile reactions Lydgate encounters from the medical establishment and townspeople, suggesting these conflicts are not unique to the present moment but reflect enduring human nature.

text:
That opposition to the New Fever Hospital which Lydgate had sketched to
Dorothea was, like other oppositions, to be viewed in many different lights. He
regarded it as a mixture of jealousy and dunderheaded prejudice. Mr. Bulstrode
saw in it not only medical jealousy but a determination to thwart himself,
prompted mainly by a hatred of that vital religion of which he had striven to
be an effectual lay representative—a hatred which certainly found pretexts
apart from religion such as were only too easy to find in the entanglements of
human action. These might be called the ministerial views. But oppositions have
the illimitable range of objections at command, which need never stop short at
the boundary of knowledge, but can draw forever on the vasts of ignorance. What
the opposition in Middlemarch said about the New Hospital and its
administration had certainly a great deal of echo in it, for heaven has taken
care that everybody shall not be an originator; but there were differences
which represented every social shade between the polished moderation of Dr.
Minchin and the trenchant assertion of Mrs. Dollop, the landlady of the Tankard
in Slaughter Lane.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces the multifaceted opposition to Lydgate's New Fever Hospital and the range of social viewpoints in Middlemarch, establishing the chapter's central conflict.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate views opposition to the Hospital as professional jealousy, while Bulstrode interprets it as religious hatred, but the narrator notes that opposition encompasses the full spectrum of ignorant objections from Dr. Minchin's moderation to Mrs. Dollop's trenchant assertion.

context: This passage opens the chapter by introducing the widespread opposition to Lydgate's proposed New Fever Hospital in Middlemarch. It establishes that different people view this opposition through different lenses—Lydgate sees jealousy and prejudice, Bulstrode sees religious hatred, while the townspeople's objections range from Dr. Minchin's measured concerns to Mrs. Dollop's passionate objections. The passage sets up the exploration of how ignorance and social position shape public opinion against Lydgate's medical innovations.

text:
Mrs. Dollop became more and more convinced by her own asseveration, that Dr.
Lydgate meant to let the people die in the Hospital, if not to poison them, for
the sake of cutting them up without saying by your leave or with your leave;
for it was a known “fac” that he had wanted to cut up Mrs. Goby, as respectable
a woman as any in Parley Street, who had money in trust before her marriage—a
poor tale for a doctor, who if he was good for anything should know what was
the matter with you before you died, and not want to pry into your inside after
you were gone. If that was not reason, Mrs. Dollop wished to know what was; but
there was a prevalent feeling in her audience that her opinion was a bulwark,
and that if it were overthrown there would be no limits to the cutting-up of
bodies, as had been well seen in Burke and Hare with their pitch-plaisters—such
a hanging business as that was not wanted in Middlemarch!

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Dollop's colorful and vivid articulation of public fear around body-snatching and dissection reveals genuine anxieties while providing comic relief through exaggeration.
enrichment.best_quote: Dr. Lydgate meant to let the people die in the Hospital, if not to poison them, for the sake of cutting them up without saying by your leave or with your leave
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Dollop expresses her conviction that Lydgate intends to dissect patients without consent, conflating his medical ambitions with the notorious Burke and Hare murders, thereby mobilizing public anxiety against him.

context: This passage presents Mrs. Dollop, the landlady of the Tankard pub in Slaughter Lane, voicing widespread public suspicions about Dr. Lydgate's medical practices. She spreads rumors that he intends to let hospital patients die or poison them in order to perform autopsies and dissections without consent. Mrs. Dollop references the real case of Mrs. Goby, whose relatives Lydgate had asked permission to autopsy after her death, and invokes the notorious Burke and Hare body-snatching murders to inflame local opinion against him. Her views, though ignorant and exaggerated, represent the common fears and prejudices of ordinary townspeople regarding Lydgate's medical innovations and anatomical investigations.

text:
And let it not be supposed that opinion at the Tankard in Slaughter Lane was
unimportant to the medical profession: that old authentic public-house—the
original Tankard, known by the name of Dollop’s—was the resort of a great
Benefit Club, which had some months before put to the vote whether its
long-standing medical man, “Doctor Gambit,” should not be cashiered in favor of
“this Doctor Lydgate,” who was capable of performing the most astonishing
cures, and rescuing people altogether given up by other practitioners. But the
balance had been turned against Lydgate by two members, who for some private
reasons held that this power of resuscitating persons as good as dead was an
equivocal recommendation, and might interfere with providential favors. In the
course of the year, however, there had been a change in the public sentiment,
of which the unanimity at Dollop’s was an index.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes the social weight of tavern opinion and shows the community's initial skepticism toward Lydgate, though shifting sentiment is implied.
enrichment.summary: The Tankard Inn, frequented by a Benefit Club, previously voted against Lydgate's appointment, but public sentiment is changing in his favor.

context: This chunk appears in the section examining public opinion about Dr. Lydgate in Middlemarch. It demonstrates how the working-class opinion at Dollop's tavern—represented by Mrs. Dollop and the Benefit Club members—initially rejected Lydgate despite his medical skill, fearing his curative powers might interfere with divine providence. The passage shows that sentiment is gradually shifting in Lydgate's favor over the course of a year, contrasting with the active hostility from established medical practitioners like Dr. Gambit and others who view him as a threatening rival.

text:
A good deal more than a year ago, before anything was known of Lydgate’s skill,
the judgments on it had naturally been divided, depending on a sense of
likelihood, situated perhaps in the pit of the stomach or in the pineal gland,
and differing in its verdicts, but not the less valuable as a guide in the
total deficit of evidence. Patients who had chronic diseases or whose lives had
long been worn threadbare, like old Featherstone’s, had been at once inclined
to try him; also, many who did not like paying their doctor’s bills, thought
agreeably of opening an account with a new doctor and sending for him without
stint if the children’s temper wanted a dose, occasions when the old
practitioners were often crusty; and all persons thus inclined to employ
Lydgate held it likely that he was clever. Some considered that he might do
more than others “where there was liver;”—at least there would be no harm in
getting a few bottles of “stuff” from him, since if these proved useless it
would still be possible to return to the Purifying Pills, which kept you alive
if they did not remove the yellowness. But these were people of minor
importance. Good Middlemarch families were of course not going to change their
doctor without reason shown; and everybody who had employed Mr. Peacock did not
feel obliged to accept a new man merely in the character of his successor,
objecting that he was “not likely to be equal to Peacock.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: A discursive exposition on how Middlemarch patients initially judged Lydgate's skill based on circumstance and digestive intuition rather than evidence; primarily narrative furniture.
enrichment.summary: Initial judgments of Lydgate's skill depended on various class and economic motives among patients, ranging from those with chronic illnesses willing to try him to respectable families reluctant to abandon their traditional physicians.

context: This passage describes the initial, tentative reception Lydgate received in Middlemarch before his skills became known. It explains how different social classes and patients formed opinions about him based on speculation rather than evidence—poorer patients and those seeking cheaper medical care were inclined to try him, while established families remained loyal to their longtime physician Mr. Peacock. The passage illustrates the community's divided and often irrational judgments about Lydgate, setting up the later developments where his actual cases and the town's gossip would significantly alter public opinion.

text:
But Lydgate had not been long in the town before there were particulars enough
reported of him to breed much more specific expectations and to intensify
differences into partisanship; some of the particulars being of that impressive
order of which the significance is entirely hidden, like a statistical amount
without a standard of comparison, but with a note of exclamation at the end.
The cubic feet of oxygen yearly swallowed by a full-grown man—what a shudder
they might have created in some Middlemarch circles! “Oxygen! nobody knows what
that may be—is it any wonder the cholera has got to Dantzic? And yet there are
people who say quarantine is no good!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: The narrator's ironic commentary on how Lydgate's modern scientific interests (oxygen, cholera) provoke ignorant suspicion, revealing the provincial resistance to scientific progress.
enrichment.best_quote: "Oxygen! nobody knows what that may be—is it any wonder the cholera has got to Dantzic? And yet there are people who say quarantine is no good!"
enrichment.summary: Lydgate's scientific knowledge, exemplified by his interest in oxygen and modern medical theory, generates anxiety in Middlemarch circles that conflate innovation with danger.

context: This passage occurs early in the chapter's discussion of how rumors about Lydgate's medical innovations spread through Middlemarch society. It illustrates how scientific terminology and modern medical practices—specifically his reference to oxygen—become distorted and sensationalized by the townspeople, who lack understanding and interpret his work through fear and ignorance. The excerpt exemplifies the gap between Lydgate's progressive medicine and the superstitious, rumor-driven objections he faces from the general population.

text:
One of the facts quickly rumored was that Lydgate did not dispense drugs. This
was offensive both to the physicians whose exclusive distinction seemed
infringed on, and to the surgeon-apothecaries with whom he ranged himself; and
only a little while before, they might have counted on having the law on their
side against a man who without calling himself a London-made M.D. dared to ask
for pay except as a charge on drugs. But Lydgate had not been experienced
enough to foresee that his new course would be even more offensive to the
laity; and to Mr. Mawmsey, an important grocer in the Top Market, who, though
not one of his patients, questioned him in an affable manner on the subject, he
was injudicious enough to give a hasty popular explanation of his reasons,
pointing out to Mr. Mawmsey that it must lower the character of practitioners,
and be a constant injury to the public, if their only mode of getting paid for
their work was by their making out long bills for draughts, boluses, and
mixtures.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces a crucial professional innovation—Lydgate's refusal to dispense drugs—that becomes a focal point of medical and social resentment, illustrating his inadvertent provocation.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate's decision not to dispense drugs offends both physicians (whose privilege it infringes) and the laity, and his hasty explanation to Mr. Mawmsey compounds the offense by implying that other doctors are mischievous.

context: This passage introduces Lydgate's controversial decision to stop dispensing drugs to his patients and charging them separately for medicines—a practice that violates medical convention in Middlemarch. It describes how this reform offends both the established physicians and apothecaries, and most crucially, explains how Lydgate's imprudent explanation of his principles to the grocer Mr. Mawmsey sets in motion a chain of miscommunication and prejudice against him throughout the town, as Mawmsey spreads a distorted version of Lydgate's views among Middlemarch's influential tradespeople.

text:
“It is in that way that hard-working medical men may come to be almost as
mischievous as quacks,” said Lydgate, rather thoughtlessly. “To get their own
bread they must overdose the king’s lieges; and that’s a bad sort of treason,
Mr. Mawmsey—undermines the constitution in a fatal way.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's direct speech reveals his idealistic but injudicious candor about professional ethics, which becomes the source of rumor and misrepresentation.
enrichment.best_quote: It is in that way that hard-working medical men may come to be almost as mischievous as quacks," said Lydgate, rather thoughtlessly. "To get their own bread they must overdose the king's lieges; and that's a bad sort of treason, Mr. Mawmsey—undermines the constitution in a fatal way."
enrichment.summary: Lydgate articulates his ethical objection to the profit motive in medicine, arguing that physicians who profit from dispensing drugs are incentivized to overprescribe.

context: Lydgate explains to Mr. Mawmsey, a grocer and town official, why he refuses to dispense drugs to his patients, arguing that the practice of charging for medications incentivizes doctors to overprescribe and harm their patients' health. This remark, made hastily and without full consideration of its audience, becomes widely misinterpreted throughout Middlemarch as Lydgate claiming that medicine itself is useless, damaging his reputation among both patients and rival physicians.

text:
Mr. Mawmsey was not only an overseer (it was about a question of outdoor pay
that he was having an interview with Lydgate), he was also asthmatic and had an
increasing family: thus, from a medical point of view, as well as from his own,
he was an important man; indeed, an exceptional grocer, whose hair was arranged
in a flame-like pyramid, and whose retail deference was of the cordial,
encouraging kind—jocosely complimentary, and with a certain considerate
abstinence from letting out the full force of his mind. It was Mr. Mawmsey’s
friendly jocoseness in questioning him which had set the tone of Lydgate’s
reply. But let the wise be warned against too great readiness at explanation:
it multiplies the sources of mistake, lengthening the sum for reckoners sure to
go wrong.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Character sketch of Mr. Mawmsey and authorial commentary on the dangers of candid explanation; reveals how Lydgate's earnestness backfires in a world of partial understanding.
enrichment.best_quote: But let the wise be warned against too great readiness at explanation: it multiplies the sources of mistake, lengthening the sum for reckoners sure to go wrong.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Mawmsey is characterized as an important grocer whose social status and vanity make him influential; Eliot warns that Lydgate's hasty explanation will compound misunderstanding.

context: This passage describes Mr. Mawmsey, an important Middlemarch grocer and overseer, during his encounter with Dr. Lydgate regarding outdoor poor relief. It characterizes Mawmsey's personality and appearance, then reflects on how his cordial questioning prompted Lydgate's injudicious explanation against dispensing drugs—a remark that will spread through town and damage Lydgate's reputation among the medical profession and laity.

text:
Lydgate smiled as he ended his speech, putting his foot into the stirrup, and
Mr. Mawmsey laughed more than he would have done if he had known who the king’s
lieges were, giving his “Good morning, sir, good-morning, sir,” with the air of
one who saw everything clearly enough. But in truth his views were perturbed.
For years he had been paying bills with strictly made items, so that for every
half-crown and eighteen-pence he was certain something measurable had been
delivered. He had done this with satisfaction, including it among his
responsibilities as a husband and father, and regarding a longer bill than
usual as a dignity worth mentioning. Moreover, in addition to the massive
benefit of the drugs to “self and family,” he had enjoyed the pleasure of
forming an acute judgment as to their immediate effects, so as to give an
intelligent statement for the guidance of Mr. Gambit—a practitioner just a
little lower in status than Wrench or Toller, and especially esteemed as an
accoucheur, of whose ability Mr. Mawmsey had the poorest opinion on all other
points, but in doctoring, he was wont to say in an undertone, he placed Gambit
above any of them.

Other medical men felt themselves more capable. Mr. Toller shared the highest
practice in the town and belonged to an old Middlemarch family: there were

facetious man, who kept a good house, was very fond of a little sporting when

It may seem odd that with such pleasant habits he should have been given to the
heroic treatment, bleeding and blistering and starving his patients, with a
dispassionate disregard to his personal example; but the incongruity favored
the opinion of his ability among his patients, who commonly observed that Mr.
Toller had lazy manners, but his treatment was as active as you could desire:
no man, said they, carried more seriousness into his profession: he was a

great favorite in his own circle, and whatever he implied to any one’s

But in this doubtful stage of Lydgate’s introduction he was helped by what we
mortals rashly call good fortune. I suppose no doctor ever came newly to a
place without making cures that surprised somebody—cures which may be called
fortune’s testimonials, and deserve as much credit as the written or printed
kind. Various patients got well while Lydgate was attending them, some even of
dangerous illnesses; and it was remarked that the new doctor with his new ways
had at least the merit of bringing people back from the brink of death. The
trash talked on such occasions was the more vexatious to Lydgate, because it
gave precisely the sort of prestige which an incompetent and unscrupulous man
would desire, and was sure to be imputed to him by the simmering dislike of the
other medical men as an encouragement on his own part of ignorant puffing. But
even his proud outspokenness was checked by the discernment that it was as
useless to fight against the interpretations of ignorance as to whip the fog;
and “good fortune” insisted on using those interpretations.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A masterful paragraph on the paradox of Lydgate's success: his actual clinical cures generate precisely the ignorant prestige he despises, creating ironic entrapment. Addresses ambition, the limits of reason, and institutional resistance with philosophical depth.
enrichment.best_quote: It was as useless to fight against the interpretations of ignorance as to whip the fog; and "good fortune" insisted on using those interpretations.

But by-and-by Nancy, in her attic, became portentously worse, the supposed
tumor having indeed given way to the blister, but only wandered to another
region with angrier pain. The staymaker’s wife went to fetch Lydgate, and he
continued for a fortnight to attend Nancy in her own home, until under his
treatment she got quite well and went to work again. But the case continued to
be described as one of tumor in Churchyard Lane and other streets—nay, by Mrs.
Larcher also; for when Lydgate’s remarkable cure was mentioned to Dr. Minchin,
he naturally did not like to say, “The case was not one of tumor, and I was
mistaken in describing it as such,” but answered, “Indeed! ah! I saw it was a
surgical case, not of a fatal kind.” He had been inwardly annoyed, however,
when he had asked at the Infirmary about the woman he had recommended two days
before, to hear from the house-surgeon, a youngster who was not sorry to vex
Minchin with impunity, exactly what had occurred: he privately pronounced that
it was indecent in a general practitioner to contradict a physician’s diagnosis
in that open manner, and afterwards agreed with Wrench that Lydgate was
disagreeably inattentive to etiquette. Lydgate did not make the affair a ground
for valuing himself or (very particularly) despising Minchin, such
rectification of misjudgments often happening among men of equal
qualifications. But report took up this amazing case of tumor, not clearly
distinguished from cancer, and considered the more awful for being of the
wandering sort; till much prejudice against Lydgate’s method as to drugs was
overcome by the proof of his marvellous skill in the speedy restoration of
Nancy Nash after she had been rolling and rolling in agonies from the presence
of a tumor both hard and obstinate, but nevertheless compelled to yield.

Here was plenty of preparation for the outburst of professional disgust at the
announcement of the laws Mr. Bulstrode was laying down for the direction of the
New Hospital, which were the more exasperating because there was no present
possibility of interfering with his will and pleasure, everybody except Lord
Medlicote having refused help towards the building, on the ground that they
preferred giving to the Old Infirmary. Mr. Bulstrode met all the expenses, and
had ceased to be sorry that he was purchasing the right to carry out his
notions of improvement without hindrance from prejudiced coadjutors; but he had
had to spend large sums, and the building had lingered. Caleb Garth had
undertaken it, had failed during its progress, and before the interior fittings
were begun had retired from the management of the business; and when referring
to the Hospital he often said that however Bulstrode might ring if you tried
him, he liked good solid carpentry and masonry, and had a notion both of drains
and chimneys. In fact, the Hospital had become an object of intense interest to
Bulstrode, and he would willingly have continued to spare a large yearly sum
that he might rule it dictatorially without any Board; but he had another
favorite object which also required money for its accomplishment: he wished to
buy some land in the neighborhood of Middlemarch, and therefore he wished to
get considerable contributions towards maintaining the Hospital. Meanwhile he
framed his plan of management. The Hospital was to be reserved for fever in all
its forms; Lydgate was to be chief medical superintendent, that he might have
free authority to pursue all comparative investigations which his studies,
particularly in Paris, had shown him the importance of, the other medical
visitors having a consultative influence, but no power to contravene Lydgate’s
ultimate decisions; and the general management was to be lodged exclusively in
the hands of five directors associated with Mr. Bulstrode, who were to have
votes in the ratio of their contributions, the Board itself filling up any
vacancy in its numbers, and no mob of small contributors being admitted to a
share of government.

context:
# Context for Chunk Location

This chunk appears at **paragraph P55**, serving as a pivotal transition point in the chapter. It marks the culmination of the extended narrative about Lydgate's struggles against professional opposition and public misunderstanding in Middlemarch. The preceding sections (P1-P54) detail how various townspeople—from Mrs. Dollop at the Tankard to the rival physicians Dr. Minchin, Mr. Toller, and Mr. Wrench—have spread rumors about Lydgate's unorthodox medical practices (refusing to dispense drugs, conducting autopsies, and using experimental methods). The chunk signals that despite these mounting hostilities, Lydgate maintains his composure and dedication to establishing the New Fever Hospital under Mr. Bulstrode's patronage. The subsequent sections (P56-P86) show Lydgate's private reflections on his professional challenges and his relationship with his wife Rosamond, particularly his admiration for Vesalius as a historical parallel to his own struggles against medical establishment opposition.

text:
“Bulstrode is nothing to me,” said Lydgate, carelessly, “except on public
grounds. As to getting very closely united to him, I am not fond enough of him
for that. But what was the other thing you meant?” said Lydgate, who was
nursing his leg as comfortably as possible, and feeling in no great need of
advice.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's dismissive response to Farebrother's warning, showing his confidence in his own judgment and his relative indifference to advice.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate assures Farebrother that Bulstrode is merely a public figure of convenience and asks for the second piece of advice.

context: Lydgate dismisses Farebrother's warning about maintaining distance from Bulstrode, claiming he has no personal attachment to him and is only associated with him on public grounds regarding the Hospital. This response comes as part of Farebrother's counsel to Lydgate to avoid becoming too entangled with Bulstrode, whose controversial reputation in Middlemarch threatens to damage Lydgate's own standing among the town's medical community.

text:
“Why, this. Take care— experto crede —take care not to get hampered about
money matters. I know, by a word you let fall one day, that you don’t like my
playing at cards so much for money. You are right enough there. But try and
keep clear of wanting small sums that you haven’t got. I am perhaps talking
rather superfluously; but a man likes to assume superiority over himself, by
holding up his bad example and sermonizing on it.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Farebrother's second crucial warning about financial entanglement; articulates the novel's central concern about how material dependency undermines idealism and independence.
enrichment.best_quote: Take care—experto crede—take care not to get hampered about money matters. I know, by a word you let fall one day, that you don't like my playing at cards so much for money. You are right enough there. But try and keep clear of wanting small sums that you haven't got.
enrichment.summary: Farebrother advises Lydgate to avoid debt, recognizing from Lydgate's own judgment about card-playing that small financial wants can corrupt character and autonomy.

context: This is Mr. Farebrother's second piece of advice to Lydgate during their confidential conversation in the study. Farebrother warns Lydgate against financial entanglement, cautioning him not to incur debts for small sums he cannot afford, while acknowledging his own hypocrisy in offering such counsel given his own habit of playing cards for money.

text:
Lydgate took Mr. Farebrother’s hints very cordially, though he would hardly
have borne them from another man. He could not help remembering that he had
lately made some debts, but these had seemed inevitable, and he had no
intention now to do more than keep house in a simple way. The furniture for
which he owed would not want renewing; nor even the stock of wine for a long
while.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's cordial but dismissive acceptance of Farebrother's advice; reveals his confidence in his own financial prudence and his recent debts.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate appreciates Farebrother's counsel but admits to recent debts he considers inevitable, and he expects his simple household expenses to remain manageable.

context: Lydgate has just received candid advice from Mr. Farebrother about avoiding financial entanglement and maintaining distance from Bulstrode's influence. This passage shows Lydgate's reflection on his existing debts and his rationalization that they are manageable and behind him, as he resolves to live more modestly going forward.

text:
Many thoughts cheered him at that time—and justly. A man conscious of
enthusiasm for worthy aims is sustained under petty hostilities by the memory
of great workers who had to fight their way not without wounds, and who hover
in his mind as patron saints, invisibly helping. At home, that same evening
when he had been chatting with Mr. Farebrother, he had his long legs stretched
on the sofa, his head thrown back, and his hands clasped behind it according to
his favorite ruminating attitude, while Rosamond sat at the piano, and played
one tune after another, of which her husband only knew (like the emotional
elephant he was!) that they fell in with his mood as if they had been melodious
sea-breezes.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A masterful portrait of Lydgate's psychological and emotional state: his idealism sustained by historical consciousness, his contentment in marriage, and his aesthetic composure. The passage captures a moment of harmony before the collisions that will destroy it.
enrichment.best_quote: A man conscious of enthusiasm for worthy aims is sustained under petty hostilities by the memory of great workers who had to fight their way not without wounds, and who hover in his mind as patron saints, invisibly helping.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate, sustained by idealism and the memory of great medical pioneers, enjoys an evening at home with Rosamond at the piano, content in simple domestic harmony.

context: Lydgate finds solace and encouragement in his scientific ideals and memories of great medical pioneers like Vesalius despite facing professional hostility and jealousy from rival doctors in Middlemarch. That evening at home, he reflects contentedly on his worthy ambitions while Rosamond plays music at the piano, creating a moment of domestic peace that sustains him through the petty conflicts threatening his career and reputation.

text:
There was something very fine in Lydgate’s look just then, and any one might
have been encouraged to bet on his achievement. In his dark eyes and on his
mouth and brow there was that placidity which comes from the fulness of
contemplative thought—the mind not searching, but beholding, and the glance
seeming to be filled with what is behind it.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A stunning physical and psychological portrait of Lydgate's composure and potential; foreshadows his vulnerability by emphasizing his apparent strength and the contingency of achievement.
enrichment.best_quote: In his dark eyes and on his mouth and brow there was that placidity which comes from the fulness of contemplative thought—the mind not searching, but beholding, and the glance seeming to be filled with what is behind it.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate's appearance at this moment suggests both achievement and the precarious foundations of success, inviting speculation about his future.

context: This passage describes Lydgate's peaceful, contemplative state at home with his wife Rosamond in the evening, after a conversation with Mr. Farebrother about the hostility he faces in town regarding the New Fever Hospital and his unorthodox medical practices. The description captures a moment of quiet confidence and intellectual absorption, as Lydgate reflects on great historical physicians like Vesalius despite the professional opposition arrayed against him in Middlemarch.

text:
Presently Rosamond left the piano and seated herself on a chair close to the
sofa and opposite her husband’s face.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief stage direction showing Rosamond's movement; primarily connective.
enrichment.summary: Rosamond leaves the piano and sits near Lydgate's face.

context: Lydgate, buoyed by his scientific ambitions and philosophical confidence despite professional hostility in Middlemarch, reflects on his work and ideals while Rosamond plays music. As she finishes, she moves closer to him on the sofa, initiating an intimate conversation about his intellectual preoccupations.

text:
“Is that enough music for you, my lord?” she said, folding her hands before her
and putting on a little air of meekness.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rosamond's playful, affectionate question; light domestic banter without depth.
enrichment.summary: Rosamond playfully addresses Lydgate, assuming a modest tone and asking if he has had enough music.

context: Rosamond asks Lydgate if he has had enough music after playing the piano for him during an intimate domestic moment at home. This occurs after Lydgate has discussed with Mr. Farebrother the professional hostility he faces in Middlemarch, and he returns home to find comfort in his wife's company and contemplation of great medical pioneers like Vesalius.

text:
“Yes, dear, if you are tired,” said Lydgate, gently, turning his eyes and
resting them on her, but not otherwise moving. Rosamond’s presence at that
moment was perhaps no more than a spoonful brought to the lake, and her woman’s
instinct in this matter was not dull.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A tender moment showing Lydgate's gentle responsiveness and Rosamond's intuitive perception of his absorption; captures the fragility of their connection.
enrichment.best_quote: Rosamond's presence at that moment was perhaps no more than a spoonful brought to the lake, and her woman's instinct in this matter was not dull.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate gently responds to Rosamond while remaining absorbed in his thoughts; the narrator notes that Rosamond intuitively recognizes her limited place in his inner preoccupations.

context: Lydgate, absorbed in contemplation of his medical ambitions and the historical anatomist Vesalius, is momentarily interrupted by his wife Rosamond's question about whether he has had enough music. His response reveals his emotional distance—her presence registers minimally against the vast preoccupation of his thoughts, though she perceptively senses his distraction.

text:
“What is absorbing you?” she said, leaning forward and bringing her face nearer
to his.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rosamond's attempt to draw Lydgate into conversation; brief and formulaic.
enrichment.summary: Rosamond leans forward and asks what is absorbing his attention.

context: Rosamond interrupts Lydgate's contemplative thoughts about Vesalius and medical innovation, asking what occupies his mind as he lies on the sofa during an evening at home.

text: He moved his hands and placed them gently behind her shoulders.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Minimal physical action; purely connective narrative.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate moves to place his hands gently behind Rosamond's shoulders.

context: Lydgate and Rosamond share an intimate moment at home in the evening. After discussing his medical challenges in town, Lydgate is relaxing on the sofa while Rosamond plays piano. When she stops playing and asks what is absorbing him, he responds by placing his hands gently behind her shoulders in a tender gesture.

text:
“I am thinking of a great fellow, who was about as old as I am three hundred
years ago, and had already begun a new era in anatomy.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's revelation of his contemplation of Vesalius; introduces the historical parallel that structures the remaining marital dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate explains that he has been thinking about Vesalius, a great anatomist from three centuries past.

context: Lydgate reflects on Vesalius while reclining on the sofa as Rosamond plays piano, expressing his admiration for historical medical pioneers who faced professional opposition despite their scientific innovations.

text:
“I can’t guess,” said Rosamond, shaking her head. “We used to play at guessing
historical characters at Mrs. Lemon’s, but not anatomists.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rosamond's inability to guess Vesalius and her gentle irony; light but revealing her limited engagement with his scientific world.
enrichment.summary: Rosamond cannot guess who Vesalius is and jokes that she is unfamiliar with anatomists.

context: Lydgate is reflecting on his medical ambitions while resting at home with his wife Rosamond. He becomes absorbed in thoughts of Vesalius, the great anatomist who revolutionized the field three centuries earlier. When Lydgate mentions Vesalius to Rosamond, she cannot guess who he is referring to, as anatomists were not part of the historical guessing games she played at Mrs. Lemon's social gatherings.

text:
“I’ll tell you. His name was Vesalius. And the only way he could get to know
anatomy as he did, was by going to snatch bodies at night, from graveyards and
places of execution.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's account of Vesalius's body-snatching; introduces the controversial method that parallels Lydgate's own dissection requests and foreshadows Rosamond's anxiety.
enrichment.best_quote: The only way he could get to know anatomy as he did, was by going to snatch bodies at night, from graveyards and places of execution."
enrichment.summary: Lydgate explains that Vesalius obtained anatomical knowledge by stealing bodies from graveyards and execution sites at night.

context: Lydgate discusses the historical anatomist Vesalius with his wife Rosamond, explaining how Vesalius had to secretly exhume bodies to advance anatomical knowledge, drawing a parallel to the current suspicions and hostility directed at Lydgate himself in Middlemarch for his medical innovations and alleged disrespect for the dead.

text:
“Oh!” said Rosamond, with a look of disgust on her pretty face, “I am very glad
you are not Vesalius. I should have thought he might find some less horrible
way than that.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rosamond's expression of disgust and preference for conventional morality; establishes the thematic gulf between scientific ambition and social propriety.
enrichment.summary: Rosamond expresses horror at Vesalius's grave-robbing and is relieved that Lydgate is not similarly inclined.

context: Lydgate is reflecting on the anatomist Vesalius, explaining to his wife Rosamond how Vesalius had to steal bodies from graveyards and execution sites to study anatomy. Rosamond expresses disgust at these methods, and Lydgate defends Vesalius's necessity to pursue scientific knowledge despite the moral compromises required.

text:
“No, he couldn’t,” said Lydgate, going on too earnestly to take much notice of
her answer. “He could only get a complete skeleton by snatching the whitened
bones of a criminal from the gallows, and burying them, and fetching them away
by bits secretly, in the dead of night.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's earnest elaboration of Vesalius's desperate methods; shows his absorption in the parallel and his inability to gauge Rosamond's anxiety.
enrichment.best_quote: He could only get a complete skeleton by snatching the whitened bones of a criminal from the gallows, and burying them, and fetching them away by bits secretly, in the dead of night."
enrichment.summary: Lydgate elaborates on Vesalius's elaborate scheme to steal criminals' bones from gallows and transport them secretly.

context: Lydgate is explaining to his wife Rosamond the historical necessity of grave-robbing for anatomical study, using the example of Vesalius, a pioneering anatomist from three hundred years prior. Rosamond has expressed disgust at such methods, but Lydgate insists there was no alternative way to obtain complete skeletal knowledge necessary for advancing anatomical science.

text:
“I hope he is not one of your great heroes,” said Rosamond, half playfully,
half anxiously, “else I shall have you getting up in the night to go to St.
Peter’s churchyard. You know how angry you told me the people were about Mrs.
Goby. You have enemies enough already.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rosamond's worried intervention connecting Vesalius's graveside activities to Lydgate's dissection requests and his growing enemies; articulates her anxiety about his reputation and safety.
enrichment.best_quote: I hope he is not one of your great heroes," said Rosamond, half playfully, half anxiously, "else I shall have you getting up in the night to go to St. Peter's churchyard. You know how angry you told me the people were about Mrs. Goby. You have enemies enough already."
enrichment.summary: Rosamond expresses concern that Vesalius not become a role model for Lydgate, alluding to his controversial dissection request and his already precarious social position.

context: Rosamond expresses concern about Lydgate's admiration for Vesalius, the anatomist who obtained bodies for dissection through grave-robbing. She fears his fascination with such methods might lead him to similar practices, especially given the townspeople's existing anger over his request to examine Mrs. Goby's body after her death.

text:
“So had Vesalius, Rosy. No wonder the medical fogies in Middlemarch are
jealous, when some of the greatest doctors living were fierce upon Vesalius
because they had believed in Galen, and he showed that Galen was wrong. They
called him a liar and a poisonous monster. But the facts of the human frame
were on his side; and so he got the better of them.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's confident response invoking Vesalius as a martyr to scientific truth opposed by institutional dogmatism; articulates his self-understanding as a reformer struggling against ignorant opposition.
enrichment.best_quote: No wonder the medical fogies in Middlemarch are jealous, when some of the greatest doctors living were fierce upon Vesalius because they had believed in Galen, and he showed that Galen was wrong. They called him a liar and a poisonous monster. But the facts of the human frame were on his side; and so he got the better of them.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate defends Vesalius as a martyr who overcame institutional opposition through the force of anatomical truth, implicitly comparing his own struggle to Vesalius's.

context: Lydgate defends his controversial medical practices and autopsy work to his wife Rosamond by drawing a parallel to Vesalius, the pioneering anatomist who faced fierce opposition from established physicians who clung to Galen's outdated theories. Lydgate argues that just as Vesalius was vindicated by empirical facts despite being called a liar and monster, he too will be proven right against the jealous "medical fogies" of Middlemarch who resist his innovations.

text: “And what happened to him afterwards?” said Rosamond, with some interest.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rosamond's brief inquiry about Vesalius's outcome; shows some interest despite her misgivings.
enrichment.summary: Rosamond asks what ultimately happened to Vesalius.

context: Rosamond asks Lydgate about the later life of Vesalius, the anatomist he has been describing to her. Lydgate had been explaining how Vesalius had to steal bodies from graveyards to study anatomy, and how he faced opposition from other doctors who believed in Galen's incorrect teachings.

text:
“Oh, he had a good deal of fighting to the last. And they did exasperate him
enough at one time to make him burn a good deal of his work. Then he got
shipwrecked just as he was coming from Jerusalem to take a great chair at
Padua. He died rather miserably.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's account of Vesalius's difficult end—harassment, self-destruction, shipwreck, and miserable death—which foreshadows Lydgate's own tragic fate.
enrichment.best_quote: He had a good deal of fighting to the last. And they did exasperate him enough at one time to make him burn a good deal of his work. Then he got shipwrecked just as he was coming from Jerusalem to take a great chair at Padua. He died rather miserably.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate recounts that Vesalius experienced continuous struggle, burned his own work in frustration, was shipwrecked, and died miserably.

context: Lydgate recounts to his wife Rosamond the tragic fate of Vesalius, the pioneering anatomist he admires, explaining how Vesalius faced fierce opposition from established medical authorities who believed in Galen's theories. Lydgate draws a parallel between Vesalius's struggles against entrenched medical dogma and his own conflicts with the jealous doctors of Middlemarch.

text:
There was a moment’s pause before Rosamond said, “Do you know, Tertius, I often
wish you had not been a medical man.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rosamond's devastating question expressing her regret that Lydgate became a doctor; crystallizes the deep incompatibility between her values and his vocation, and articulates her class anxiety about his professional choice.
enrichment.best_quote: Do you know, Tertius, I often wish you had not been a medical man.
enrichment.summary: Rosamond confesses to Lydgate her wish that he had chosen a different profession.

context: This moment occurs late in the chapter when Lydgate and Rosamond are at home together in the evening. Lydgate is contemplatively stretched on the sofa, thinking about the great anatomist Vesalius and the obstacles he faced, while Rosamond plays piano. After he has earnestly described Vesalius's difficulties and ultimate tragic fate, Rosamond expresses her wish that Lydgate had chosen a different profession, revealing her discomfort with the medical profession and its social standing.

text:
“Nay, Rosy, don’t say that,” said Lydgate, drawing her closer to him. “That is
like saying you wish you had married another man.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's pained protest comparing the wish to a wish she had married another man; reveals the depth of his attachment to his vocation and his hurt at her rejection.
enrichment.best_quote: Nay, Rosy, don't say that," said Lydgate, drawing her closer to him. "That is like saying you wish you had married another man.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate is hurt by Rosamond's remark, arguing that to dislike his vocation is to dislike the core of his identity.

context: Lydgate responds to Rosamond's wish that he had not become a medical man, defending his profession and drawing an analogy to her marriage choice, as tensions emerge between his dedication to medicine and her social aspirations.

text:
“Not at all; you are clever enough for anything: you might easily have been
something else. And your cousins at Quallingham all think that you have sunk
below them in your choice of a profession.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rosamond's articulation of class status anxiety: Lydgate had other options but chose a profession her wealthy cousins deem beneath them.
enrichment.best_quote: Your cousins at Quallingham all think that you have sunk below them in your choice of a profession.
enrichment.summary: Rosamond notes that Lydgate's Quallingham cousins believe he has degraded himself by becoming a doctor.

context: Rosamond expresses her dissatisfaction with Lydgate's choice of medicine as a profession, suggesting he could have pursued something more prestigious, and notes that his cousins view his medical career as beneath their social standing.

text:
“The cousins at Quallingham may go to the devil!” said Lydgate, with scorn. “It
was like their impudence if they said anything of the sort to you.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's scornful dismissal of his cousins' judgment; brief and emphatic but reveals class resentment.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate dismisses his cousins' opinions as impertinent and assumes they made disparaging remarks to Rosamond.

context: Lydgate responds with indignation when Rosamond suggests his medical profession is beneath the social standing of his wealthy cousins at Quallingham, dismissing their snobbish judgment while defending his choice of career despite the town's hostility toward him.

text:
“Still,” said Rosamond, “I do  not  think it is a nice profession, dear.”
We know that she had much quiet perseverance in her opinion.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rosamond's persistent objection to medicine as a profession; demonstrates her fixed class prejudice and hints at her quiet but immovable resistance.
enrichment.best_quote: Still," said Rosamond, "I do not think it is a nice profession, dear."
enrichment.summary: Rosamond reiterates her conviction that medicine is not a respectable profession, demonstrating her persistent quiet resistance to Lydgate's vocation.

context: Lydgate and Rosamond discuss his medical career at home. Despite his passionate defense of medicine as "the grandest profession in the world," Rosamond persistently expresses her disapproval of his choice to become a doctor, viewing it as beneath the social standing of his family at Quallingham.

text:
“It is the grandest profession in the world, Rosamond,” said Lydgate, gravely.
“And to say that you love me without loving the medical man in me, is the same
sort of thing as to say that you like eating a peach but don’t like its flavor.
Don’t say that again, dear, it pains me.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's passionate defense of medicine as 'the grandest profession' and his metaphor of the peach; articulates his vocational idealism and his pain at Rosamond's rejection of a core part of his identity.
enrichment.best_quote: It is the grandest profession in the world, Rosamond," said Lydgate, gravely. "And to say that you love me without loving the medical man in me, is the same sort of thing as to say that you like eating a peach but don't like its flavor. Don't say that again, dear, it pains me."
enrichment.summary: Lydgate insists that medicine is the grandest profession and argues that to love him is to love the medical aspect of his identity, using the metaphor of a peach and its flavor.

context: Lydgate defends his choice of medicine as a profession to his wife Rosamond, who has expressed doubt about his career and suggested he might have chosen something else. He argues passionately that medicine is noble work and that she cannot claim to love him while rejecting the core of his identity and values.

text:
“Very well, Doctor Grave-face,” said Rosy, dimpling, “I will declare in future
that I dote on skeletons, and body-snatchers, and bits of things in phials, and
quarrels with everybody, that end in your dying miserably.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rosamond's playful reconciliation with mock agreement; demonstrates her manipulative charm and her way of evading genuine confrontation while maintaining her underlying position.
enrichment.best_quote: Very well, Doctor Grave-face," said Rosy, dimpling, "I will declare in future that I dote on skeletons, and body-snatchers, and bits of things in phials, and quarrels with everybody, that end in your dying miserably."
enrichment.summary: Rosamond responds with playful sarcasm, sarcastically agreeing to embrace the disreputable and tragic elements associated with his vocation.

context: Rosamond responds playfully to Lydgate's passionate defense of medicine as "the grandest profession in the world," sarcastically listing the unpleasant aspects of his medical work—anatomical study, body-snatching history, laboratory specimens, and professional conflicts—that she has criticized throughout their conversation about his career choice and the hostility he faces in Middlemarch.

text:
“No, no, not so bad as that,” said Lydgate, giving up remonstrance and petting
her resignedly.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lydgate's capitulation and resignation; shows his inability to sustain principled disagreement and his pragmatic choice of domestic peace over honest argument.
enrichment.summary: Lydgate abandons his remonstrance and yields to Rosamond's playfulness through physical affection.

context: This closing line concludes Lydgate's conversation with his wife Rosamond about his medical profession. After Rosamond jokingly expresses disapproval of his career and its dangers, Lydgate abandons his attempts to convince her of medicine's nobility and instead affectionately placates her, revealing the tension between his professional ambitions and domestic harmony.

text:
Pues no podemos haber aquello que queremos, queramos aquello que podremos.
   
Since we cannot get what we like, let us like what we can get.— Spanish
Proverb .

enrichment.interest_rationale: A Spanish epigraph offering a moral precept about accepting what is available—functional but not distinctive.
enrichment.best_quote: Since we cannot get what we like, let us like what we can get.
enrichment.summary: A proverb about accepting circumstances rather than pursuing impossible desires.

context: This epigraph opens the chapter and thematically frames the tensions between idealism and pragmatism that drive the narrative. It relates particularly to Will Ladislaw's political work with Mr. Brooke and the Reform movement, as well as to the broader theme of characters accepting practical circumstances rather than pursuing perfect ideals—exemplified in Will's acceptance of editorial work at the "Pioneer" despite it not being his loftiest ambition, and in Lydgate's pragmatic collaboration with Bulstrode despite moral reservations.

text:
While Lydgate, safely married and with the Hospital under his command, felt
himself struggling for Medical Reform against Middlemarch, Middlemarch was
becoming more and more conscious of the national struggle for another kind of
Reform.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes the chapter's political context and Lydgate's tension between medical and national reform, showing his limited influence in Middlemarch.
enrichment.summary: While Lydgate manages the Hospital and pursues medical reform, Middlemarch becomes preoccupied with the national question of political reform.

context: This chunk opens the chapter by establishing a parallel between Lydgate's personal struggle for medical reform and the broader national political movement for parliamentary reform that is gaining momentum in Middlemarch. It sets up the tension between individual ambitions and collective social change that drives the subsequent narrative, introducing Will Ladislaw's emerging role as a political editor and reformer.

text:
By the time that Lord John Russell’s measure was being debated in the House of
Commons, there was a new political animation in Middlemarch, and a new
definition of parties which might show a decided change of balance if a new
election came. And there were some who already predicted this event, declaring
that a Reform Bill would never be carried by the actual Parliament. This was
what Will Ladislaw dwelt on to Mr. Brooke as a reason for congratulation that
he had not yet tried his strength at the hustings.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Provides necessary historical and political context (Lord John Russell's Reform Bill) and introduces Will Ladislaw's role as political actor, but remains largely expository.
enrichment.summary: Middlemarch experiences new political animation around Reform debates; Will advises Mr. Brooke that a new election is likely and he should wait to stand.

context: The chunk is part of a discussion of the broader political context affecting Middlemarch during the period of parliamentary Reform debate. It serves as a transition from describing Lydgate's personal struggles to introducing the national political ferment that provides the backdrop for Will Ladislaw's new work as editor of the "Pioneer" newspaper and his collaboration with Mr. Brooke. The chunk establishes that political Reform is creating new opportunities and divisions in the town, setting up the subsequent conversation between Will and Brooke about political strategy and the necessity of supporting Reform measures.

text:
“Things will grow and ripen as if it were a comet year,” said Will. “The public
temper will soon get to a cometary heat, now the question of Reform has set in.
There is likely to be another election before long, and by that time
Middlemarch will have got more ideas into its head. What we have to work at now
is the ‘Pioneer’ and political meetings.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Will's vivid imagery ('comet year,' 'cometary heat') and confident political strategy are engaging; reveals his role at the Pioneer and optimism about reform momentum.
enrichment.best_quote: The public temper will soon get to a cometary heat, now the question of Reform has set in.
enrichment.summary: Will assures Mr. Brooke that public opinion will intensify around Reform and outlines his strategy: strengthen the Pioneer newspaper and organize political meetings.

context: Will Ladislaw encourages Mr. Brooke to embrace political reform through the 'Pioneer' newspaper and public meetings, arguing that growing public sentiment will drive political change and create opportunities for reform before the next election.

text:
“Quite right, Ladislaw; we shall make a new thing of opinion here,” said Mr.
Brooke. “Only I want to keep myself independent about Reform, you know; I don’t
want to go too far. I want to take up Wilberforce’s and Romilly’s line, you
know, and work at Negro Emancipation, Criminal Law—that kind of thing. But of
course I should support Grey.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reveals Mr. Brooke's cautious reformism and conflicted principles; his name-dropping of Wilberforce and Romilly is characteristic but politically uncertain.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Brooke professes support for Grey and selective reforms (emancipation, criminal law) but hesitates about full commitment to change.

context: Mr. Brooke discusses his political strategy with Will Ladislaw regarding the Reform movement. He expresses his desire to remain independent while supporting Reform efforts, stating he prefers to focus on specific causes like Negro Emancipation and Criminal Law reform—following the example of Wilberforce and Romilly—rather than embracing comprehensive constitutional change. He affirms his support for Grey while maintaining he does not want to radically alter the balance of the constitution.

text:
“If you go in for the principle of Reform, you must be prepared to take what
the situation offers,” said Will. “If everybody pulled for his own bit against
everybody else, the whole question would go to tatters.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Will articulates a coherent political principle about unified reform, but the exchange is relatively brief and abstract.
enrichment.best_quote: If everybody pulled for his own bit against everybody else, the whole question would go to tatters.
enrichment.summary: Will argues that piecemeal reform will fail unless all reformers act in concert.

context: Will Ladislaw advises Mr. Brooke that supporting political Reform requires accepting pragmatic compromises rather than pursuing narrow individual interests, arguing that fragmented efforts would undermine the broader reform movement.

text:
“Yes, yes, I agree with you—I quite take that point of view. I should put it in
that light. I should support Grey, you know. But I don’t want to change the
balance of the constitution, and I don’t think Grey would.”

Will was not displeased with that complimentary comparison, even from Mr.
Brooke; for it is a little too trying to human flesh to be conscious of
expressing one’s self better than others and never to have it noticed, and in
the general dearth of admiration for the right thing, even a chance bray of
applause falling exactly in time is rather fortifying. Will felt that his
literary refinements were usually beyond the limits of Middlemarch perception;
nevertheless, he was beginning thoroughly to like the work of which when he
began he had said to himself rather languidly, “Why not?”—and he studied the
political situation with as ardent an interest as he had ever given to poetic
metres or mediaevalism. It is undeniable that but for the desire to be where
Dorothea was, and perhaps the want of knowing what else to do, Will would not
at this time have been meditating on the needs of the English people or
criticising English statesmanship: he would probably have been rambling in
Italy sketching plans for several dramas, trying prose and finding it too
jejune, trying verse and finding it too artificial, beginning to copy “bits”
from old pictures, leaving off because they were “no good,” and observing that,
after all, self-culture was the principal point; while in politics he would
have been sympathizing warmly with liberty and progress in general. Our sense
of duty must often wait for some work which shall take the place of
dilettanteism and make us feel that the quality of our action is not a matter
of indifference.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A magnificent passage of Eliot's psychological insight into Will's character: his need for recognition, his nascent commitment to reform motivated partly by desire for Dorothea, and the philosophical generalization about duty replacing dilettantism. Unmissable highlight.
enrichment.best_quote: Our sense of duty must often wait for some work which shall take the place of dilettanteism and make us feel that the quality of our action is not a matter of indifference.
enrichment.summary: Eliot reveals that Will's commitment to political reform, while genuine, is partly motivated by his desire to be near Dorothea; the narrator reflects on how purposeful work elevates us beyond mere self-indulgence, and how Will would otherwise have frittered away his talents in artistic dabbling.

context: This passage comes after Will Ladislaw's conversation with Mr. Brooke about political reform and the Reform Bill. Mr. Brooke has just complimented Will's eloquence, comparing him to Burke and wishing he could secure him a pocket-borough seat in Parliament. The passage provides crucial insight into Will's character and motivations, revealing that his commitment to political work and reform is largely driven by his desire to be near Dorothea rather than by genuine conviction, and that without this motivation, he would have remained a dilettante artist in Italy. It establishes a key theme: that meaningful work and duty can transform an otherwise aimless person into someone purposeful.

loftiest thing which he had once dreamed of as alone worthy of continuous

glow of public spirit. In spite of Mr. Casaubon and the banishment from Lowick,
he was rather happy; getting a great deal of fresh knowledge in a vivid way and

Keck, the editor of the “Trumpet,” in asserting that Ladislaw, if the truth

to see a strip of a fellow, with light curls round his head, get up and
speechify by the hour against institutions “which had existed when he was in
his cradle.” And in a leading article of the “Trumpet,” Keck characterized
Ladislaw’s speech at a Reform meeting as “the violence of an energumen—a
miserable effort to shroud in the brilliancy of fireworks the daring of
irresponsible statements and the poverty of a knowledge which was of the
